english: I have a dog (I'm raising a dog)
usage: Polite; the everyday way to say you own/raise a pet
Progressive; stresses you currently have one
Swap 강아지 → 고양이 for a cat
examples: 저 강아지 키워요.
I have a dog.
키우다 ('to raise') is the verb for owning any pet, not 있다 alone
집에서 고양이 두 마리 키워요.
I have two cats at home.
Count pets with 마리: 한 마리, 두 마리
강아지 키운 지 3년 됐어요.
I've had my dog for 3 years.
-(으)ㄴ 지 ... 됐어요 = 'it's been ... since I started'
nuance: 키우다 literally means 'to raise / bring up', and it is THE verb Koreans use for having a pet — you 'raise' a dog the same way you raise a child or grow a plant. Saying 강아지 키워요 sounds completely natural and warm; it implies you care for the animal, not just that one exists nearby. This is polite-neutral 존댓말, fine with anyone; drop to 강아지 키워 with friends. The big English-speaker trap is translating 'I have a dog' as 강아지 있어요 — that is grammatical but means 'a dog exists / there is a dog (here)', so it sounds like you're reporting a dog is present, not that you own one as a pet; for ownership-as-caretaking, Koreans say 키워요. A second trap: don't use 가지다 ('to possess') as 강아지 가지고 있어요 — that frames a living animal like an object you hold, which feels cold and odd. Also note 강아지 technically means 'puppy' but in speech Koreans call any dog, even an old one, 강아지 affectionately; the neutral word for 'dog' is 개, but 개 can sound blunt, so 강아지 is the friendly default. Count animals with the counter 마리 and native numbers: 한 마리, 두 마리.

mistakes: Saying 강아지 있어요 to mean 'I have a dog'.
있어요 means 'exists / is here', so it reports a dog's presence, not that you own and care for one. For having a pet, say 강아지 키워요.
Saying 강아지 가지고 있어요.
가지다 ('to possess/hold') treats the animal like an object. A pet is 'raised', so use 키우다: 강아지 키워요.
Counting pets with 개 (the general counter).
Animals take the counter 마리: 강아지 두 마리. 개 is the counter for inanimate items (and also the word 'dog'), so 강아지 두 개 sounds wrong.

usage: 반말; what you say to your dog or a close friend
Polite, to a person (e.g. a partner)
Let's go (out) to take a walk
examples: 우리 산책 가자!
Let's go for a walk!
Said to your dog; dogs learn the word 산책 fast
비 와서 오늘은 산책 못 가.
It's raining, so no walk today.
못 가 = 'can't go' (circumstance), softer than 안 가
강아지 산책 좀 시키고 올게요.
I'll go walk the dog and come back.
산책시키다 = to walk the pet; you make IT walk
nuance: 산책 is 'a (leisurely) walk / stroll' (Sino-Korean 散策), and 산책 가다 = 'go for a walk' is the daily ritual every Korean dog owner knows. There's a crucial split English speakers miss: 산책하다 / 산책 가다 means YOU go for a walk, while 산책시키다 (causative -시키다) means you WALK THE DOG — you make the animal take its walk. So to your dog you cheerfully say 산책 가자 ('let's go for a walk', joining it), but to another person you'd report 강아지 산책시켜요 ('I walk the dog'). Mixing these up — saying 강아지를 산책해요 — is wrong, because 산책하다 is intransitive (you can't 'walk' the dog with it); you need the causative 산책시키다 to put the dog as the object. To your dog, 반말 is normal (you don't use 존댓말 to a pet); 산책 가자 or just 산책! is what owners actually say. Note 산책 is for relaxed walking; if you mean brisk exercise-walking, that's 걷기 운동, and hiking a mountain is 등산 — don't call a mountain hike 산책. The set phrase 산책 가자 is also a sweet way to invite a friend out, but with a person use polite 산책 가요 unless they're close.

Using 존댓말 to your own dog.
Koreans speak 반말 to pets. 산책 가요 to your dog sounds unnatural; say 산책 가자.
Calling a mountain hike 산책.
산책 is a gentle stroll. Hiking a mountain is 등산. 산에 산책 가요 sounds off — say 등산 가요.

english: What kind of food do you feed (your pet)?
usage: What food do you feed it?
Polite; asking another owner or a vet
Asking staff at a pet shop
examples: 강아지한테 사료 뭐 먹여요?
What food do you feed your dog?
한테 marks the pet as the receiver of food
저희 고양이는 이 사료만 먹어요.
My cat only eats this food.
From the pet's side, use 먹다 ('eats'), not 먹이다
수의사 선생님, 사료 어떤 거 먹이는 게 좋아요?
Doctor, what food is best to feed?
먹이는 게 좋아요 = 'it's good to feed' (asking advice)
nuance: 사료 is the specific word for animal feed / pet kibble (Sino-Korean 飼料) — you do NOT call it 밥 or 음식 when you mean commercial pet food, though owners affectionately say 밥 먹자 ('let's eat') to the pet. The verb pair here trips up English speakers: 먹다 = '(the pet) eats', but 먹이다 = '(I) feed / make eat' (causative). So 'I feed the dog kibble' is 강아지한테 사료를 먹여요, while 'the dog eats kibble' is 강아지가 사료를 먹어요. Using 먹다 where you mean 'feed' (e.g. 강아지 사료 먹어요 when you mean YOU feed it) blurs who's doing what. The particle on the pet is 한테 (or formal 에게) — the dog is the recipient: 강아지한테 먹여요; saying 강아지를 먹여요 alone can sound like you're 'feeding ON the dog'. This phrase is polite-neutral, perfect for chatting with another owner, a 펫숍 (pet shop) clerk, or a vet. Note 어떤 거 ('what kind / which one') invites a category answer (brand, wet vs. dry), whereas 뭐 ('what') is more open; both are natural. Don't confuse 사료 (dry/commercial feed) with 간식 ('treats/snacks') — asking about 사료 is about the staple diet.

Commercial pet food is 사료. 음식 is human food; use 사료 when asking a vet or shop: 사료 어떤 거 먹여요?
Saying 강아지가 사료 먹여요 to mean 'I feed the dog'.
먹이다 (feed) needs the feeder as subject and the pet as 한테: (제가) 강아지한테 사료를 먹여요. 강아지가 ... 먹여요 mixes up who eats and who feeds.
Marking the pet with 를 alone: 강아지를 먹여요.
The fed animal takes 한테/에게 for the recipient: 강아지한테 사료를 먹여요. 강아지를 먹여요 sounds like feeding on the dog.

english: I'll fill up your water bowl
usage: 반말, talking to your pet / casually
갈아 주다 = swap for fresh water
I should wash the food bowl
examples: 물그릇 비었네, 채워 줄게.
The water bowl's empty — I'll fill it.
비다 = 'to be empty'; 채우다 = 'to fill'
고양이 물은 매일 갈아 줘야 돼요.
You should change a cat's water every day.
갈아 주다 = replace with fresh, not just top up
밥 줬으니까 이제 물그릇만 채우면 돼.
I fed it, so now I just need to fill the water bowl.
...면 돼 = '(I) just need to ...'
nuance: 물그릇 = 'water bowl' (물 'water' + 그릇 'bowl/dish'), and 밥그릇 = 'food bowl' — these compound words are how owners refer to pet dishes. The verb choices matter: 채우다 = 'to fill (up)', 갈다 = 'to change/replace' (swap old water for fresh), and 비우다 = 'to empty'. Koreans distinguish 물 채워 줘 ('fill it up', add water) from 물 갈아 줘 ('change the water', dump and replace) — for hygiene you usually 갈아 주다 daily, so don't just say 채우다 if you mean fresh water. The -아/어 줄게 ending ('I'll do it for you') and -아/어 줘 ('do it for me') express doing the action as a favor, which is the warm register owners naturally use toward pets (in 반말). The English-speaker trap is reaching for generic 만들다 or 넣다 — 'put water in' is fine as 물 넣어 줘, but the idiomatic care-verbs are 채우다/갈다. Also note 그릇 is the bowl; don't confuse it with 접시 ('flat plate'), which isn't used for a pet's water. Since you're speaking to or about your pet, 반말 with -줄게/-줘 is natural; to a person helping you, say 물 좀 채워 주세요.

채우다 just adds water to what's there. To replace stale water with clean, say 물 갈아 줘 ('change the water').
Using 접시 for the water dish.
접시 is a flat plate. A pet's bowl is 그릇: 물그릇, 밥그릇.
Over-formal 채워 드릴게요 toward your pet.
Honorifics like 드리다 are for elevating people. To a pet, 반말 is normal: 물그릇 채워 줄게.

english: I have to pick up the poop
usage: I have to pick up the poop
Polite-neutral; 응가 = cute word for poop
반말; 똥 is blunter than 응가
Did you grab a poop bag?
오줌 (을) 싸다 = to pee; 쌌어 = peed
examples: 산책할 때 응가 꼭 치워야 돼요.
You must pick up poop when walking.
꼭 = 'definitely/without fail' — it's a rule and courtesy
배변봉투로 똥 치우고 왔어.
I picked up the poop with a bag and came back.
배변봉투로 = 'using a waste bag' (instrument 로)
우리 강아지 아직 화장실 못 가려요.
My dog isn't potty-trained yet.
화장실 가리다 = to be house-trained / control toileting
nuance: 치우다 = 'to clear away / clean up / pick up', the exact verb for scooping pet waste — not 청소하다 ('to clean a room/surface'), which is too broad for picking up a single poop. For the waste itself, 응가 is a soft, slightly babyish word ('poop / number two') that owners and parents use; 똥 is the plain, blunter 'poop / crap' (fine in 반말 but earthy); the clinical term is 대변. A 배변봉투 ('defecation bag') is the poop bag you must carry on walks — picking up after your dog is both etiquette and, in many places, the law. The English-speaker trap is saying 응가 잡다 — 잡다 means 'to grab/catch (a moving thing)', wrong here; you 치우다 ('clear away') waste. Another trap: don't say 응가 만들다. For peeing, 오줌 (을) 싸다 or politely 소변 보다; 'potty-trained' is 화장실(을) 가리다 (lit. 'to distinguish the bathroom'). This phrase is polite-neutral; with friends you'd say 똥 치워야 돼. Because 응가/똥 are casual, in a vet or formal context use 대변/소변.

잡다 = grab/catch (something moving). For cleaning up waste use 치우다: 응가 치워야 돼요.
Using 청소하다 for scooping a single poop.
청소하다 = clean (a whole area). For picking up pet waste, the verb is 치우다.
Saying 똥 in a formal vet conversation.
똥 is blunt/casual. In a clinic, use 대변 (feces) and 소변 (urine): 대변 색이 이상해요.

english: Does it need to get vaccinated?
usage: I got it the rabies shot
주사 맞히다 = have (it) get a shot
examples: 강아지 예방접종 언제 맞아야 돼요?
When should my dog get vaccinated?
맞다 (passive 'receive a shot') — the pet 'gets' the shot
이번에 광견병 예방접종 맞혔어요.
I had it get the rabies vaccine this time.
맞히다 (causative) = I make it receive the shot
접종 기록 카드 가지고 오세요.
Bring the vaccination record card.
접종 기록 = vaccination record (kept by the clinic)
nuance: 예방접종 = 'preventive vaccination' (예방 'prevention' + 접종 'inoculation'), the umbrella word for pet shots; 광견병 = 'rabies', a key annual one. The verb is the classic learner minefield: 주사/접종을 맞다 = '(the patient) receives a shot' (it's the way Korean says 'get a shot', not literally 'be hit'), while 맞히다 (causative) = '(I) have/make it receive a shot'. So your dog 주사를 맞아요 ('gets the shot'), and you 주사를 맞혔어요 ('had it get the shot'). English speakers wrongly use the active 'do' verb and say 주사를 해요 or import 'inject' as 주사하다 about themselves — for receiving, it's 맞다. Saying 주사를 때려요 (맞다's other meaning is 'be struck', so learners over-correct to 'hit') is wrong. This is polite-neutral, exactly right for the 동물병원 (animal hospital/vet). Note 동물병원 literally 'animal hospital' is the standard word for a vet clinic — there's no separate word like 'vet's office'; the vet themselves is 수의사(선생님). Keep the 접종 기록 (vaccine record); clinics ask for it. The -아야 돼요? frame ('must / should?') politely asks about requirement.

Confusing 맞다 (the pet gets it) with 맞히다 (you have it get it).
강아지가 주사를 맞아요 = the dog gets the shot. (제가) 강아지한테 주사를 맞혔어요 = I had it vaccinated. Pick by who's doing what.
Calling the vet clinic 병원 only.
병원 alone implies a human hospital. The vet is 동물병원: 동물병원 가야 돼요.

usage: I'd like to book the clinic
Saying it to the clinic / on the phone
진료 받다 = receive a medical exam
examples: 내일 동물병원 예약했어요.
I made a vet appointment for tomorrow.
예약하다 = to reserve/book (an appointment)
강아지 진료 예약하려고 전화했어요.
I called to book my dog's exam.
진료 = medical consultation/exam at a clinic
접수처에서 이름이랑 증상 말씀하세요.
Tell them the name and symptoms at reception.
접수처 = the reception desk; 증상 = symptoms
nuance: 예약하다 = 'to reserve / book' (an appointment, table, ticket), and 동물병원 예약 is how you book a vet visit. Don't confuse the steps Korean clinics use: 예약 = the booking made in advance, 접수 = checking in / registering when you arrive, and 진료 = the actual exam/consultation. So you 예약하다 by phone, 접수하다 at the desk, then 진료(를) 받다 ('receive an exam'). English speakers often collapse these and say only 'appointment', but using 접수 on arrival and 진료 for the exam makes you sound fluent. Note 진료 받다 uses 받다 ('to receive') — you receive the exam; saying 진료해요 about yourself is wrong, since 진료하다 is what the DOCTOR does. This phrase is polite-neutral. A frequent trap: 'reservation' as 예약 is right, but don't say 약속 — 약속 is a 'promise / social plans (with a person)', not a booked appointment with a business. For symptoms tell the desk the 증상 (symptoms). The clinic may say 보호자분 ('guardian', i.e. you the owner) — Koreans call pet owners 보호자, literally 'protector/guardian', in medical settings.

The clinic may say 보호자분 ('guardian', i.e. you the owner) — Koreans call pet owners 보호자, literally 'protector/guardian', in medical settings.

Don't confuse the steps Korean clinics use: 예약 = the booking made in advance, 접수 = checking in / registering when you arrive, and 진료 = the actual exam/consultation. So you 예약하다 by phone, 접수하다 at the desk, then 진료(를) 받다 ('receive an exam'). English speakers often collapse these and say only 'appointment', but using 접수 on arrival and 진료 for the exam makes you sound fluent.

진료하다 is what the doctor does (examines). The patient side is 진료(를) 받다: 진료 받으러 왔어요.

Korean clinics have you 접수 (check in) at the desk first. Say 접수 먼저 할게요 on arrival, then wait to be called.

english: Where does it hurt? / What's wrong?
usage: What the vet asks; you describe the symptom
안 먹어요 = refuses food (a key symptom)
토하다 = to throw up; 계속 = continuously
examples: 우리 강아지가 어제부터 밥을 안 먹어요.
My dog hasn't eaten since yesterday.
어제부터 = 'since yesterday' — give onset time
고양이가 자꾸 토하고 기운이 없어요.
The cat keeps throwing up and has no energy.
기운이 없다 = to be lethargic / have no energy
여기를 만지면 아파하는 것 같아요.
It seems to hurt when I touch here.
아파하다 = to show pain (about an animal/other); -것 같다 = 'seems'
nuance: 아프다 = 'to be sick / hurt / in pain', and 어디가 아파요? ('where does it hurt / what's wrong?') is what the 수의사 asks — you'll mainly ANSWER by describing symptoms. A subtle but important point: 아프다 describes YOUR OWN felt pain, but for an animal (or another person whose pain you observe), Korean uses 아파하다 ('to act like it's in pain / show pain') — so 강아지가 아파해요 ('the dog seems to be in pain'), not 강아지가 아파요 in careful speech, though casually owners do say 아파요 too. Key symptom verbs: 토하다 (vomit), 설사하다 (have diarrhea), 절다 (limp), 기운이 없다 (be lethargic), 안 먹다 (won't eat). English speakers often say only 'sick' and stop — but Korean vets expect the onset (언제부터, 'since when') and the concrete symptom. Don't translate 'feel sick' as 아픈 느낌 — just say 아파요 or name the symptom. Also 토하다 (vomit) is not 뱉다 ('to spit out') — a dog 토해요 when it throws up. This frame is polite-neutral. Give the time with -부터 ('from/since'): 어제부터, 아침부터.

Vets need specifics. Add the symptom and onset: 어제부터 밥을 안 먹고 토해요.

Strictly, you feel 아프다; an animal you observe 아파하다 (shows pain). 강아지가 아파해요 is the careful form.
Saying 뱉어요 to mean 'it vomits'.
뱉다 = spit out (deliberately). Vomiting is 토하다: 자꾸 토해요.

examples: 저희 고양이는 중성화 수술 했어요.
My cat is spayed/neutered.
중성화 (中性化) applies to both male and female pets
중성화 하면 성격이 좀 차분해져요.
Neutering makes them a bit calmer.
차분해지다 = to become calm/settled
수술한 데 핥지 못하게 넥카라 씌웠어요.
I put a cone on so it can't lick the incision.
넥카라 (neck collar) = the cone; 씌우다 = put (it) on
nuance: 중성화 = 'neutering / spaying' (中性化, lit. 'making neuter'), and 중성화 수술 = the operation; conveniently this single word covers BOTH males and females, so you don't need separate English-style words for 'neuter' vs. 'spay' — just 중성화. The verb 수술(을) 하다 = 'to have/do surgery'; from the owner's side 중성화 수술 했어요 ('had it done') is normal even though technically the vet performs it — Korean lets the responsible person say 했어요. The English-speaker trap is searching for 거세 ('castration') — 거세 is the literal/blunt term and feels clinical or even harsh for a pet; everyday owners and clinics say 중성화. Another trap: 'fixed' has no literal Korean match; don't say 고쳤어요 ('repaired/fixed') — that means you fixed a broken object, not the procedure. This phrase is polite-neutral and a very common get-to-know-your-pet question among owners (중성화 했어요?). Related care vocabulary: 넥카라 (the protective cone, from 'neck collar'), 회복 ('recovery'), 핥다 ('to lick' — pets lick the 수술 부위, the surgical site, so the cone prevents it). Keep 수술 with 하다/받다.

고치다 = repair a broken thing. For the procedure say 중성화 수술 했어요, not 고쳤어요.

중성화 covers spaying females too. You don't switch words by sex — 암컷도 중성화 한다 ('females are also neutered').

usage: Polite; ask BEFORE petting a stranger's dog
examples: 강아지 만져도 돼요? 안 물어요?
Can I pet the dog? Does it bite?
Always ask both before approaching a strange dog
저희 강아지는 안 물어요, 순해요.
My dog doesn't bite, it's gentle.
순하다 = good-natured; reassures the asker
낯선 사람 보면 좀 짖어요.
It barks a bit at strangers.
짖다 = to bark (≠ 물다 'to bite')
nuance: 물다 = 'to bite', and 물어요? ('does it bite?') plus 만져도 돼요? ('may I pet it?') are the two phrases you say BEFORE touching anyone's dog — essential etiquette. -아도 돼요? = 'is it okay if I...? / may I...?', the standard permission frame; 만지다 = 'to touch/pet'. The English-speaker trap is confusing the animal-sound verbs: 물다 = bite, but 짖다 = 'to bark' and 으르렁거리다 = 'to growl' — a dog that 짖어요 (barks) isn't necessarily going to 물다 (bite). Don't say 물기 해요 or import 'bite' oddly; the plain verb 물다 conjugates 물어요. Also note 물다 sounds like 묻다 ('to ask' / 'to bury' / 'to get stained') — keep them apart: 물어요 from 물다 = 'bites', but 물어요 from 묻다 can mean 'asks'; context (a dog) makes it clear, but learners sometimes mis-hear. To describe temperament: 순하다 (gentle), 사납다 (fierce/aggressive), 무서워하다 (to be scared of). This is polite-neutral, ideal with strangers. Petting culture: many Koreans will let you pet their dog if you ask, but always ask 만져도 돼요? first — reaching out silently is considered rude and can startle the dog.

Always ask first: 만져도 돼요? 물어요? Reaching out silently can startle the dog and annoy the owner.

Both can surface as 물어요, but from different verbs. With a dog, 물어요? = 'does it bite?' Keep the base verbs straight.

english: Please put it on a leash
examples: 여기서는 목줄 꼭 해 주세요.
Please keep it leashed here.
꼭 = without fail; leashing in public is the law
대형견은 입마개도 해야 돼요.
Large dogs must also wear a muzzle.
대형견 = large-breed dog; 입마개 = muzzle
엘리베이터에서는 안아 주시거나 목줄 짧게요.
In the elevator, hold it or keep the leash short.
안다 = to hold in arms; 짧게(요) = keep it short
nuance: 목줄 = 'leash / collar-lead' (목 'neck' + 줄 'cord/line'), the standard word; 가슴줄 / 하네스 = a 'harness' (chest lead). 목줄 (을) 하다 or 채우다 = 'to put on / fasten a leash'. In Korea, leashing your dog in public is legally required, and certain large or 'dangerous' breeds must also wear an 입마개 ('muzzle', 입 'mouth' + 마개 'plug/stopper') — so 목줄 해 주세요 and 입마개 해야 돼요 are phrases you may hear or need. The verb 채우다 here means 'to fasten/buckle' (same verb as filling a bowl, but with a leash it's 'fasten') — 목줄 채우다 = clip the leash on. The English-speaker trap is calling a leash 끈 (a generic 'string/strap') — understandable but 목줄 is the specific term. Don't use 묶다 ('to tie up') for normal leashing — 묶다 implies tethering the dog to a post; routine leash-walking is 목줄 하다/잡다 ('hold the lead'). This phrase as 해 주세요 is a polite request to another owner; 안다 ('to hold in one's arms') is what you do with a small dog in tight spaces like elevators. Korean apartment etiquette: in elevators many owners 안아요 (carry) or keep the 목줄 짧게 (short) out of courtesy.

Forgetting the muzzle term 입마개.
Some large breeds legally need a muzzle: 입마개. Don't invent 입 가리개; the standard word is 입마개.

english: It was so cute that I adopted it
usage: Polite; 입양 = adoption (of a pet or child)
I brought it from a shelter
examples: 작년에 고양이 한 마리 입양했어요.
I adopted a cat last year.
입양하다 = to adopt; 한 마리 = one (animal)
유기견 보호소에서 강아지 데려왔어요.
I brought a dog home from a shelter.
보호소 = (animal) shelter; 데려오다 = bring home
펫숍에서 분양받는 것보다 입양이 좋아요.
Adopting beats buying from a pet shop.
분양받다 (buy/obtain) contrasted with 입양 (adopt)
nuance: 입양 = 'adoption' (入養), used for both adopting a child AND taking in a pet — so 입양했어요 is the warm word for giving a rescue animal a home. There's a meaningful contrast Korean draws: 입양 (adopt, usually from a 보호소 'shelter' or rescuing a 유기견/유기묘 'abandoned dog/cat') vs. 분양 (literally 'parceling out') which is how you 'get' a pet from a breeder or 펫숍, often by paying — owners say 분양받았어요 for that. Animal-welfare-minded Koreans say 사지 말고 입양하세요 ('don't buy, adopt'). The verb 데려오다 = 'to bring (a person/animal) home/along' — you 데려오다 a dog from the shelter; this is different from 가져오다 ('bring an object'), and using 가져오다 for a living animal sounds wrong/cold. The English-speaker trap is 사다 ('to buy') — while pets can be bought, calling it 사다 in conversation can sound blunt; 분양받다 or 입양하다 are the natural verbs. Also don't say 채택하다 — that's 'to adopt (a plan/proposal)', not a living being. This phrase is polite-neutral. Related: 보호소 (shelter), 임시보호 ('temporary fostering'), 유기 ('abandonment').

mistakes: Saying 가져왔어요 about bringing a pet home.
가져오다 is for objects. For a living animal use 데려오다: 보호소에서 데려왔어요.
Using 채택하다 for adopting an animal.
채택하다 = adopt a plan/idea. Adopting a pet (or child) is 입양하다: 강아지를 입양했어요.
Calling shelter adoption 분양.
분양 implies obtaining (often buying) from a breeder/shop. Taking in a rescue is 입양; the source is a 보호소.

usage: Asking a pet's age; answer in 살
Is it a boy or a girl?
examples: 우리 강아지, 완전 우리 애기예요.
My dog is totally my baby.
완전 (totally, slangy intensifier) shows affection
우리 집 막내, 세 살이에요.
Our youngest, three years old.
Pets are counted as 막내 (youngest family member)
남자아이예요, 이름은 콩이예요.
It's a boy, his name's Kong-i.
-이 suffix on a pet's name is endearing (콩 → 콩이)
nuance: Korean pet owners overwhelmingly treat pets as family, so they call them 애기/아기 ('baby'), 우리 막내 ('our youngest'), or 우리 가족 ('our family') — 우리 애기예요 ('this is my baby') is genuine, everyday speech, not baby-talk you'd be embarrassed by. Note the all-important 우리 ('our/my'): Koreans say 우리 강아지, 우리 고양이 ('our dog/cat') rather than 제 강아지, treating the pet as shared family — using 제 (my, humble-possessive) for a beloved pet can sound oddly distancing. Owners also refer to a pet's sex as 남자아이 / 여자아이 ('boy / girl') rather than the blunt animal terms 수컷 ('male') / 암컷 ('female'), which are used in clinical/breeding contexts; calling your cute pet 수컷 in casual chat sounds like a livestock report. Ages take native numbers + 살: 세 살. The endearing -이 suffix attaches to names ending in a consonant (콩 → 콩이, 별 → 별이). The English-speaker trap is over-formal 제 애완동물 ('my pet animal') — 애완동물 is a correct dictionary word but feels stiff and a bit dated; the warmer modern term is 반려동물 ('companion animal'), and in affectionate speech people just say 우리 애기/강아지. This register is casual-affectionate; with strangers you still keep 존댓말 endings (예요).

수컷/암컷 (male/female) are clinical/livestock terms. Owners say 남자아이/여자아이 for a pet's sex in friendly conversation.
Using 애완동물 thinking it's the warm word.
애완동물 is correct but stiff/dated. The modern, kinder term is 반려동물; affectionately, just 우리 애기/강아지.

english: It sheds so much (the fur falls out a lot)
usage: Polite-neutral; 털 빠지다 = fur falls out/sheds
examples: 요즘 털이 너무 많이 빠져요.
It's shedding a ton lately.
빠지다 (intransitive) = (fur) falls out, comes off
털갈이 철엔 매일 빗질해 주는 게 좋아요.
In shedding season, brush it daily.
철 = season; 빗질하다 = brush the coat
내일 강아지 미용 맡겼어요.
I dropped my dog off for grooming tomorrow.
미용 맡기다 = entrust (the pet) for grooming
nuance: 털 = 'fur / hair (of an animal)', and 빠지다 = 'to fall out / come off' (intransitive) — so 털이 빠져요 = 'the fur sheds / falls out'. The grammar trap for English speakers is voice: shedding is described with the intransitive 빠지다 ('fur falls out by itself'), with 털 as the SUBJECT (털이 빠져요), NOT 'the dog sheds fur' transitively. Don't say 강아지가 털을 빠져요 — wrong, because 빠지다 isn't transitive; either 강아지 털이 빠져요 or 강아지가 털이 많이 빠져요 (double-subject, very natural). 털갈이 = the seasonal 'coat change / molt' (털 + 갈이 'changing'), and 털갈이 철 ('shedding season') is when it's worst. Grooming words: 빗질(하다) = brushing, 미용 = the professional grooming/haircut (you 맡기다 'entrust' your pet to a 애견미용실 'dog grooming salon'), 목욕(시키다) = bathing (causative — you bathe the pet). The English-speaker trap is using 머리카락 ('head hair, human') for animal fur — animals have 털, only humans have 머리카락. Also don't say 떨어지다 ('to drop/fall') for shedding — 빠지다 is the verb for hair/fur coming out. This phrase is polite-neutral, common small-talk among owners and with groomers.

Using 머리카락 for animal fur.
머리카락 is human head hair. Animal fur/hair is 털: 털이 많이 빠져요.
Saying 털이 떨어져요 for shedding.
떨어지다 = drop/fall (off a surface). Hair/fur coming out is 빠지다: 털이 빠져요.

english: I have to register my pet (microchip/registration)
usage: I have to register my pet
Polite; 동물등록 = the legal pet registration
Did you get the microchip done?
I put on the ID tag
인식표 = external ID tag (the other option)
examples: 강아지는 법적으로 동물등록 해야 돼요.
Dogs must be registered by law.
법적으로 = 'legally'; dog registration is mandatory in Korea
동물병원에서 내장칩으로 동물등록 했어요.
I registered with a microchip at the vet.
내장칩으로 = 'by/with the microchip' (method 으로)
등록 안 하면 과태료 나올 수 있어요.
You can get a fine if you don't register.
과태료 = an administrative fine; 나오다 = to be issued
nuance: 동물등록 = 'animal registration' (動物登錄), the legally required registration of your dog with the local government — a real obligation newcomers often don't know about, with a 과태료 ('fine') for skipping it. You register via two methods: 내장칩 ('internal/implanted microchip', injected at the 동물병원) or an 외장형 인식표 ('external ID tag'); the microchip is most common. You receive a 동물등록증 ('registration certificate'). The verb is 등록(을) 하다 = 'to register'; 동물등록 했어요 = 'I registered (the pet)'. The English-speaker trap is using 가입하다 ('to sign up / join', for memberships, insurance, services) for registration — 가입 is for subscribing to something you join, whereas official record-registration is 등록; so it's 동물등록 했어요, never 동물 가입했어요. Another trap: 칩 (chip) alone is understood, but the set term is 내장칩 (internal chip) vs. 인식표 (tag). This phrase is polite-neutral, exactly what you'd say to a vet or another owner. Note 과태료 (administrative fine) differs from 벌금 (a criminal/court fine) — pet-registration penalties are 과태료. Currently only dogs are legally required to register; cat registration is voluntary in most areas.

mistakes: Saying 동물 가입했어요 for registering a pet.
가입하다 is for joining/subscribing (memberships, insurance). Official registration is 등록하다: 동물등록 했어요.
Thinking registration is optional for dogs.
Dog 동물등록 is legally required in Korea, with a 과태료 (fine) for non-compliance. Do it at the 동물병원 (microchip) or a 동사무소.
Saying 벌금 for the non-registration penalty.
벌금 is a criminal/court fine. An administrative penalty like this is 과태료: 과태료 나올 수 있어요.

english: How much was the vet bill?
usage: How much was the vet bill?
How much is the exam fee?
펫보험 = pet insurance; 들다 = to take out (insurance)
나오다 used for a bill 'coming out' to an amount
examples: 오늘 진료비 얼마 나왔어요?
How much was today's vet bill?
얼마 나왔어요 = 'how much did it come out to'
검사까지 해서 십만 원 나왔어요.
With the tests, it came to 100,000 won.
검사 = (medical) test; -까지 해서 = 'including ... '
동물병원은 보험이 안 돼서 좀 비싸요.
Vets are pricey since insurance doesn't apply.
보험이 안 되다 = insurance doesn't cover it
nuance: 진료비 = 'consultation / treatment fee' (診療費), the vet bill; -비 is the Sino-Korean suffix for 'fee/cost' (교통비 transport, 식비 food, 병원비 hospital). The natural verb for a bill is 나오다 ('to come out / be issued') — 얼마 나왔어요? = 'how much did it come out to?' — which English speakers rarely guess; they tend to say 얼마였어요? ('how much was it?'), understandable but less idiomatic for a calculated total. Korean vet care is largely NOT covered by national health insurance (that's only for humans), so bills can be high and surprising; 펫보험 ('pet insurance') exists but you must 들다/가입하다 ('take it out / sign up') in advance. The English-speaker trap is 가격 ('price') — 가격 is for the price tag on goods; for a service fee/bill, the word is 비(용) or 진료비. Another trap: don't confuse 진료비 (the exam/treatment fee) with 약값 ('medicine cost') — they may be itemized separately. Currency reminder: amounts use Sino-Korean numbers + 원 (만 원 = 10,000 won), and Koreans count in 만 (ten-thousands), so 십만 원 = 100,000 won. This phrase is polite-neutral, fine with staff at checkout or with another owner comparing costs.

mistakes: Asking 가격 얼마예요? for a vet bill.
가격 is the price of goods. A service fee/bill is 진료비 or 비용: 진료비 얼마 나왔어요?
Saying 얼마였어요? for the total bill.
Understandable, but for a calculated bill Koreans say 얼마 나왔어요? ('how much did it come out to'). Use 나오다 for bills.
Assuming national insurance covers the vet.
건강보험 covers humans only; vet care isn't covered, so it's pricey. For coverage you need private 펫보험, taken out in advance.

usage: Can I bring my dog in?
애견 동반 = accompanied by a dog
examples: 저기요, 여기 강아지 데리고 들어가도 돼요?
Excuse me, can I bring my dog in?
데리고 들어가다 = go in with the dog (live being → 데리고)
반려동물 동반 가능한 카페 찾고 있어요.
I'm looking for a pet-friendly café.
동반 가능 = accompaniment possible (pet-friendly)
여기는 케이지에 넣으면 출입 돼요.
Here it's allowed if it's in a carrier.
케이지/이동장 = carrier; 넣다 = put (it) in
nuance: 반려동물 = 'companion animal', the modern, respectful umbrella term for pets (반려 'companion' + 동물 'animal'), now standard on signs and in media — much warmer than the older 애완동물 ('pet animal', lit. 'plaything animal'). 출입 = 'entry / coming and going' (出入), so 출입 돼요? = 'is entry allowed?'; 동반 = 'accompanying', so 반려동물 동반 가능 = 'pets may accompany (you)' = pet-friendly, the exact phrase on café/store signs. To say you bring your pet in, use 데리고 들어가다 ('go in WITH (a living being)') — the verb 데리다 ('to take/bring a person/animal along') is for the living; using 가지고 들어가다 ('bring an object in') for your dog sounds wrong and a bit dehumanizing. The English-speaker trap is asking 'allowed' with 허락 ('permission/consent') as 허락돼요? — 허락 is for personal permission between people; for public access the natural phrase is 출입 돼요? or 들어가도 돼요?. Many indoor places require a 이동장 / 케이지 ('carrier') or that small dogs be carried; cafés may be 노키즈/펫 프렌들리. This phrase is polite-neutral. Note: 동반 sounds formal/sign-like; in speech 강아지 데리고 가도 돼요? is the everyday spoken version.

mistakes: Asking 허락돼요? for whether pets are allowed.
허락 is personal permission/consent. For public entry, ask 출입 돼요? or 들어가도 돼요?: 반려동물 출입 돼요?
Saying 강아지 가지고 들어가도 돼요?
가지고 (가지다) is for objects. For a living animal use 데리고: 강아지 데리고 들어가도 돼요?
Using 애완동물 on/about modern pet-friendly places.
Signs and polite speech use 반려동물 (companion animal). 애완동물 sounds dated; prefer 반려동물 동반.

english: It passed away (crossed the rainbow bridge)
usage: Gentle euphemism for a pet's death
Soft way to say a pet died
What you say to a grieving owner
examples: 우리 강아지가 어제 무지개다리 건넜어요.
My dog crossed the rainbow bridge yesterday.
무지개다리(를) 건너다 = the pet euphemism for dying
많이 힘드시겠어요, 위로의 말 전해요.
You must be hurting — my condolences.
위로의 말 = words of comfort (to the bereaved owner)
반려동물 장례식장도 있어요.
There are pet funeral homes too.
장례식장 = funeral hall; pet funerals exist in Korea
nuance: 무지개다리(를) 건너다 = 'to cross the rainbow bridge', the same tender euphemism English uses, and the most common gentle way Koreans speak of a pet's death; 하늘나라(에) 가다 ('go to heaven/the sky country') is another soft option. You generally AVOID the blunt 죽었어요 ('it died') when comforting a grieving owner — that's factually correct but cold; the euphemisms show respect for how deeply Koreans grieve pets (펫로스 증후군 = 'pet loss syndrome' is a recognized concept). To express condolences to the owner, 많이 힘드시겠어요 ('you must be having a hard time') or 위로의 말 전해요 ('I offer words of comfort') are warm and appropriate; the formal funeral phrase 삼가 고인의 명복을 빌어요 (traditionally for people) is increasingly used for pets too. The English-speaker trap is translating 'put to sleep / euthanize' carelessly — that's 안락사 (安樂死), a heavy clinical word; don't blurt it in casual sympathy. Another: don't say 잃어버렸어요 ('I lost it') to mean the pet died — 잃어버리다 means you misplaced/lost track of it (it ran away), a different, confusing meaning. This register is gentle 존댓말. Korea now has 반려동물 장례식장 ('pet funeral homes') and cremation services, so these aren't just figures of speech.

It's correct but cold. Use the gentle 무지개다리 건넜어요 or 하늘나라 갔어요 when comforting someone.

Blurting 안락사 as casual sympathy.
안락사 (euthanasia) is a heavy clinical term. Don't introduce it lightly; offer comfort: 많이 힘드시겠어요.
